authors: Di Pietro, F., Haustein, E., Conte, A., D'Adamo, G. & Winterhager, V.
title: EU Budget: The crowd-in effects
venue: JRC Working Papers on Territorial Modelling and Analysis 2026-06
method: synthetic control (country-level) for the RRF; local projections for ESIF
outcomes: total, public and private investment (capital formation)
headline: Synthetic control shows a positive and increasing effect of the RRF on total investment from 2022 onward, driven mainly by private investment (abstract gives no point estimate).
summary_plain: EU recovery money appears to have raised investment in recipient countries, and most of the extra investment came from private firms rather than governments.
quality: Causal design (synthetic control), but few treated units and the RRF hit all EU states at once, so donor pool and timing are hard; Commission in-house research.
interested_party: European Commission (JRC) evaluating an EU instrument

title: Assessing the impact of the EU's Recovery and Resilience Facility on institutional quality: a Bayesian synthetic control approach
method: Bayesian synthetic control on Worldwide Governance Indicators, data to 2024
headline: Finds robust, economically meaningful RRF-induced improvements in institutional quality in Italy; evidence for other main beneficiaries ranges from suggestive to limited.
summary_plain: The recovery fund seems to have improved the quality of government institutions in Italy, but the evidence for other big recipient countries is weak.
period_geography: Italy, Spain, other main RRF beneficiaries; 2021-2024
quality: Causal design but country-level, short post-period, and WGI are perception-based indicators; authors say too early for firm conclusions.

authors: Accetturo, A., Baltrunaite, A., Lazzaro, E. & Mancini, A. L.
title: Do Incentives and Organizational Innovations Affect the Performance of Public Administrations? Lessons from the Italian NRRP
method: within- and across-municipality variation in NRRP-funded vs other public works contracts (difference-in-differences-type design)
outcomes: speed of procurement awarding, start and progress of works
headline: The NRRP significantly improved procurement awarding and higher upfront liquidity sped the start of works, but no appreciable effect on the subsequent progress of works.
summary_plain: Italy's recovery plan made town halls quicker at awarding public works contracts and starting construction, but did not make the building itself go faster.
quality: Credible quasi-experimental design on administrative contract data; authors are Bank of Italy economists; single country.

authors: Ferri, G., Menghini, M. & Pini, M.
title: Does the NRRP speed up firms' Twin Transition? Empirical evidence from Italy
method: firm survey of almost 3,000 Italian firms; probit-type regressions with instrumental-variables robustness
outcomes: firm green and digital (twin transition) investment; firm performance
headline: Firms activating NRRP projects are more likely to start and to continue twin-transition investment, especially in disadvantaged segments and areas; results robust to IV.
summary_plain: Italian firms that took part in recovery-plan projects were more likely to invest in going green and digital.
quality: Survey-based and early; selection into NRRP projects is a concern despite IV; one co-author is from the Italian Treasury.

authors: Fernández Cerezo, A., Puente Díaz, S. & Veiga Duarte, R.
title: Weak business investment in Spain following the pandemic: an analysis based on the Banco de España Business Activity Survey
method: special module of the Banco de España Business Activity Survey (EBAE), descriptive statistics
headline: 45% of firms with NGEU-funded projects said they would not have made the investments without the funds and 31% would have made only part of them; additionality lower for green investment.
summary_plain: Most Spanish firms that got EU recovery money say they would not have invested as much without it, though the effect is weaker for green projects.
quality: Self-reported counterfactual from firms, not a causal estimate; large representative central-bank survey.

authors: Havlik, A., Heinemann, F., Helbig, S. & Nover, J.
title: Dispelling the shadow of fiscal dominance? Fiscal and monetary announcement effects for euro area sovereign spreads in the corona pandemic
method: event study regressions on government bond spreads of ten euro countries
headline: Only the Next Generation EU announcement among fiscal measures had a smaller but statistically significant spread-reducing effect; PEPP had much larger effects.
summary_plain: Announcing the EU recovery fund (of which the RRF is the core) slightly lowered borrowing costs for weaker euro countries, though ECB bond buying mattered far more.
quality: Clean high-frequency event study, but measures the NGEU announcement (before the RRF Regulation), not the Regulation's implementation.

title: On the Impact of Next Generation EU Funds: A Regional Synthetic Control Method Approach
headline: Finds NGEU funds raised Spanish regional GDP per capita in 2022 relative to a no-NGEU counterfactual (abstract gives no magnitude; 2023-24 projected).
summary_plain: Spanish regions appear to have grown a little faster in 2022 because of EU recovery funds.
quality: Weak: unclear donor pool (all EU regions treated), very early and partly projected; unpublished working paper; author flags caution.

title: Support from the Recovery and Resilience Facility for the digital transition in EU member states (Special report 13/2025)
method: performance audit: document review, surveys of member states, sample of 27 digital measures in DK, FR, IT, LU, RO; milestone completion analysis
outcomes: digital spending allocation, milestones and targets, results of digital measures
headline: All member states met the 20% digital spending target, but more than one third of final milestones and targets in the sample were inadequate or unambitious and results could be assessed for only 5 of 15 completed measures; a 'missed opportunity'.
summary_plain: Auditors found countries met the rule to spend a fifth of recovery money on digital, but often not on their biggest digital weaknesses, and progress is poorly measured.
quality: Independent audit with structured sample; qualitative-plus-counts, not causal.

title: RRF support for an improved business environment (Special report 21/2025)
method: performance audit of business-environment reforms across all RRPs and 25 sampled reforms in BG, ES, CY, AT
outcomes: coverage of country-specific recommendations; outputs and results of reforms
headline: Two thirds of 2019-2020 business-environment sub-CSRs were addressed by RRPs, but almost half only marginally and none in full; only one third of completed sampled reforms showed significant results.
summary_plain: The recovery fund's business reforms tackled some of the EU's recommendations, but rarely fully, and only a third of finished reforms showed real results.
period_geography: EU-27; BG, ES, CY, AT; Feb 2020-Apr 2025
quality: Independent audit; structured assessment with counts; small reform sample.

authors: Darvas, Z., Welslau, L. & Zettelmeyer, J.
title: The EU Recovery and Resilience Facility falls short against performance-based funding standards
method: structured content analysis of milestones and targets in seven national recovery plans (input/output/result classification)
outcomes: use of result vs input/output indicators in national plans
headline: Input indicators make up more than half of all indicators for Germany, almost half for France and over a third for the Netherlands and Spain, while Finland, Italy and Romania use many result indicators.
summary_plain: Bruegel found that many recovery plans pay out for money spent or things built rather than for real results, which undercuts the claim that the fund is performance-based.
period_geography: DE, FR, ES, FI, IT, NL, RO; plans as adopted 2021-2022
quality: Descriptive design analysis of plans, not of outcomes; early.
interested_party: Bruegel is funded partly by EU member states and corporate members; no specific position on the RRF

authors: Ecorys, CEPS, CSIL, NIESR & Wavestone (for DG ECFIN)
title: Study supporting the mid-term evaluation of the Recovery and Resilience Facility
method: mixed-method evaluation: interviews and surveys of national coordination bodies, case studies, macro-model (NiGEM) estimates
headline: Estimates GDP 0.4% higher in 2022 and unemployment 0.2 pp lower than without RRF spending; flags implementation delays and administrative burden.
summary_plain: An independent consortium hired by the Commission judged that the recovery fund lifted EU output a little in 2022 but faced delays and red tape.
quality: Macro effect is model-based, not estimated from outcome data; underpins the Commission's own mid-term evaluation SWD (already listed), so partly overlapping; commissioned by the Commission.
interested_party: Commissioned by the European Commission (DG ECFIN)

title: Report on the effectiveness of the implementation of the single European emergency number '112' (COM(2024) 575)
venue: European Commission, report under Article 109(4) EECC
method: statistical monitoring: Member State questionnaire (COCOM) data for 2023
outcomes: use of 112, handset-based caller location (AML), access for persons with disabilities
headline: 112 accounted for 62% of all emergency calls in 2023; 25 Member States had AML-enabled PSAPs by Sept 2024 but only 8 provide handset location for roaming users.
summary_plain: Use of the EU-wide 112 emergency number has grown and most countries can now locate mobile callers automatically, but not when people are roaming, and disabled users still lack equal access.
quality: Official monitoring data on an EECC obligation (Art. 109); descriptive, self-reported by Member States; Commission reporting on its own framework.
interested_party: European Commission reporting on implementation of its own legislation

authors: Gineikytė-Kanclerė, V., Klimavičiūtė, L., Kudzmanaitė, B., Lechardoy, L. et al. (PPMI & Open Evidence for DG GROW)
title: Study on evaluation of the Regulation (EU) 2019/1150 on promoting fairness and transparency for business users of online intermediation services (the P2B Regulation): final report
method: survey of 1,068 business users in 8 Member States (non-probability panel), review of T&Cs of 300 platforms, 300+ interviews, focus groups
outcomes: platform compliance with transparency/redress rules; business-user experience
headline: Full alignment of platform T&Cs with the Regulation is rare (e.g. only 22% of 290 platforms disclosed info on additional distribution channels); 62.2% of business users reported at least one issue but only 22% of them took action.
summary_plain: The Commission's external evaluators found that online platforms only patchily follow the P2B rules and that most small businesses do not know about or use the complaint routes.
quality: Large structured compliance review plus survey; opt-in survey not representative; external study underlying the Commission's 2023 review (SWD already listed), so partly overlapping.
interested_party: Commissioned by the European Commission (DG GROW)

title: Onderzoek naar ervaring van zakelijke gebruikers van online platforms met algemene voorwaarden (Study into experiences of business users on online platforms with general terms and conditions)
venue: ACM (Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets)
method: survey of 400 business users on four platforms
outcomes: awareness of P2B rights; suspensions without reasons; clarity of T&Cs; satisfaction
headline: Two in three business users were unaware of the P2B Regulation; 27% of those suspended/restricted/terminated in the past two years never received reasons in advance; one in four dissatisfied with treatment.
summary_plain: The Dutch regulator found most sellers on online platforms don't know their P2B rights, and over a quarter of those who were suspended were never told why beforehand.
quality: Regulator-commissioned survey, moderate sample, four platforms only; descriptive.

authors: Lidiard, J., Vereschak, O., Gibbs, T. & Anderljung, M.
title: Delays to Frontier AI in the EU and UK: Analysis of 375 LLM Releases by Meta, Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic
method: dataset of 375 LLM releases (June 2018-May 2026) with coded causes of EU/UK delays
outcomes: delays and non-releases of AI models in the EU relative to the US
headline: 11% of model releases were delayed or not released in the EU (7% in UK); of 68 cases, 56 attributed mainly to regulation, chiefly data protection, with no strong evidence that the AI Act caused delays.
summary_plain: Some AI models reached Europe late or not at all, mostly because of data-protection rules; the researchers found no clear sign the AI Act itself caused delays so far.
quality: Careful descriptive coding of public sources; causes inferred, GPAI obligations covered only ten months and not yet enforceable; not peer-reviewed.
interested_party: GovAI is a philanthropy-funded AI governance institute; generally supportive of frontier AI regulation

authors: Guldimann, P., Spiridonov, A., Staab, R., Jovanović, N., Vero, M., Vechev, V., Gueorguieva, A.-M., Balunović, M., Konstantinov, N., Bielik, P., Tsankov, P. & Vechev, M.
title: COMPL-AI Framework: A Technical Interpretation and LLM Benchmarking Suite for the EU Artificial Intelligence Act
method: benchmark-based compliance measurement of 12 LLMs against AI Act requirements
outcomes: model performance on AI Act-derived technical requirements (robustness, safety, fairness, etc.)
headline: Evaluating 12 prominent LLMs, finds shortcomings especially in robustness, safety, diversity and fairness; none fully meet the Act's requirements as technically interpreted.
summary_plain: Researchers tested 12 major AI chatbots against a technical reading of the AI Act and found none fully up to standard, especially on safety and fairness.
quality: Measurement depends on authors' own technical interpretation; pre-application of GPAI rules; co-authors at LatticeFlow AI, a compliance vendor.
interested_party: Co-authored by LatticeFlow AI, which sells AI compliance tools

authors: Gutierrez, E. F., Rykaczewski, M. & Vulcheva, M.
title: European Union's AI Act: Protecting the Public at the Cost of Innovation?
method: event study of stock market reactions to AI Act legislative events, with cross-sectional moderators (country AI investment, firm size, R&D intensity)
outcomes: abnormal stock returns of EU firms
headline: Negative EU-wide abnormal returns around initial and cost-increasing AI Act events, stronger in high-AI-investment countries, high-risk industries and R&D-intensive firms; larger firms fare better.
summary_plain: Share prices of European firms fell when the AI Act was proposed or tightened, especially for research-heavy and smaller firms, suggesting investors expected higher costs.
quality: Event study measures investor expectations, not realised effects; event contamination possible. Abstract read via Crossref record (SSRN page blocked).

title: Jedes vierte Unternehmen beschäftigt sich mit dem AI Act (One in four companies is dealing with the AI Act)
method: representative telephone survey of 602 German firms (20+ employees), June-July 2024
outcomes: awareness of and engagement with the AI Act; perceived effects; need for support
headline: Only 24% of German firms had engaged with the AI Act (3% in depth), 24% had never heard of it, and 69% said they need help to comply.
summary_plain: Shortly after the AI Act took effect, only a quarter of German companies had looked into it and a quarter had never heard of it.
quality: Representative survey but press-release level detail; measures awareness/perceptions not costs; industry association.
interested_party: Bitkom is the German digital industry association, lobbying on the AI Act

title: Littler European Employer Survey Report 2025
method: survey of 400+ European business leaders, in-house lawyers and HR executives
outcomes: self-assessed preparedness for AI Act compliance
headline: Just 18% of respondents say their organisations are very prepared to comply with the AI Act and 20% not at all prepared, essentially unchanged from 2024.
summary_plain: Fewer than one in five European employers feel very ready for the AI Act's rules.
quality: Self-selected respondents, self-assessed readiness; employment-law firm with commercial interest in compliance advice.
interested_party: Employment law firm selling compliance advice
